title: Avalon
composer: Al Jolson, B. G. DeSylva, Vincent Rose
origin: American Tin Pan Alley song of 1920, taken up as a flag-waver by the trad-jazz, swing and gypsy-jazz repertoires

pd.detail: First published 1920 by Jerome H. Remick & Co., New York; words and music credited to Al Jolson, B. G. DeSylva and Vincent Rose.
pd.sourceEdition: Jolson / DeSylva / Rose, 'Avalon', 1920 piano/vocal sheet, Jerome H. Remick & Co.; changes follow the common trad-jazz lead-sheet reduction of that chorus, not any later recorded arrangement.
pd.notes: Chart only: changes and form, no melody and no lyrics. The 1920 sheet is in cut time; encoded here as 4/4 at half the written tempo per the v1 meter policy. Chorus strain only -- the seldom-played 1920 verse strain is omitted because its changes are not certain. Simplifications: the final-bar beats-3-4 V7 turnaround (C7) is omitted since looping back to the A section supplies four bars of C7 anyway; no other sub-bar moves exist in the standard chart. In 1921 G. Ricordi & Co. successfully sued over the chorus melody's resemblance to an aria from Puccini's Tosca (1900); both works are now US public domain, so no encumbrance remains.

notes: Thirty-two-bar chorus in four eight-bar phrases, A A B C. The signature is the opening: four full bars sitting on the V7 before resolving home, twice in a row -- a built-in tension-release vamp that solos love. B lifts through I7 to IV, darkens to iv, and settles back on I; C is the classic II7 - V7 - I run home with four bars of tonic to land on. A staple up-tempo jam vehicle of the trad-jazz and gypsy-jazz books; ride the Tag as an out-chorus and stack repeats.
